patient.chief_complaint: Two months of progressive word-finding difficulty and personality change
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Deborah Marston is a 52-year-old right-handed woman and high school English teacher who was referred to the neurology service by her primary care physician after two months of progressive word-finding difficulty and personality changes noted by her family. Her husband reports that the first noticeable change was approximately two months ago when she began misplacing common words during dinner conversations — something highly unusual for a woman who has taught literature for 24 years and has always been exceptionally articulate. Initially, the family attributed this to stress and fatigue related to the school year. Over the following weeks, however, the word-finding difficulty became more prominent and was accompanied by a subtle but unmistakable change in her personality. Her husband describes her as becoming increasingly apathetic and emotionally flat, quite unlike her previously warm and expressive demeanor. She stopped initiating plans with friends, which was out of character, and on several occasions became unusually irritable over trivial matters. Approximately six weeks ago, she began experiencing headaches that she described as a dull, persistent pressure predominantly on the left side, worse in the morning upon waking and sometimes associated with mild nausea. She attributed these to tension headaches and increased her use of over-the-counter ibuprofen without significant relief. Three weeks ago, her daughter noticed that she struggled to help with a crossword puzzle, something the two of them had enjoyed together for years, and that she seemed to stare blankly for brief moments. There has been no witnessed seizure activity, though the family is uncertain whether these brief staring episodes could represent seizures. She denies any visual changes, though on directed questioning she admits that she occasionally has difficulty seeing things on her right side when driving, leading her to stop driving two weeks ago. She has lost approximately 4 kg of weight over the past two months without intentional dieting, which she attributes to reduced appetite. Her primary care physician ordered an outpatient MRI that revealed a left temporal lobe lesion, prompting urgent referral and admission.

mri.impression: Irregular heterogeneously enhancing left temporal mass measuring 3.8 x 2.9 x 3.1 cm with surrounding vasogenic edema and mild mass effect. The enhancement pattern is atypical — not the classic ring enhancement of glioblastoma, but the infiltrative borders and restricted diffusion at the enhancing margin raise concern for a high-grade glial neoplasm. The lesion involves the superior and middle temporal gyri with extension toward the insular cortex, placing it in proximity to language-associated cortex. No additional intracranial lesions identified to suggest metastatic disease. Differential diagnosis includes high-grade glioma (glioblastoma or anaplastic astrocytoma), lower-grade glioma with early anaplastic transformation, CNS lymphoma, and less likely tumefactive demyelination

tissue_diagnosis.impression: Integrated diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 (left temporal lobe). The layered report is what the WHO CNS5 classification requires — histology, grade and molecular findings combined — and it is what converts a radiological suspicion into a diagnosis that determines treatment. Imaging cannot substitute for it, and the molecular result changes the protocol, not merely the label.

results.title: Radiotherapy plus Concomitant and Adjuvant Temozolomide for Glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.key_finding: Addition of temozolomide to radiotherapy for newly diagnosed glioblastoma improved median survival from 12.1 to 14.6 months and 2-year survival from 10.4% to 26.5%. This 'Stupp protocol' became the standard of care.

results.title: Effects of radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide versus radiotherapy alone on survival in glioblastoma: 5-year analysis (EORTC-NCIC)
results.authors: Stupp R, Hegi ME, Mason WP, et al.
results.key_finding: Long-term follow-up confirmed durable benefit of combined temozolomide-radiotherapy. MGMT promoter methylation was the strongest predictor of benefit from temozolomide (5-year OS 13.8% vs 5.2% in unmethylated tumors).

results.title: A randomized trial of bevacizumab for newly diagnosed glioblastoma (RTOG 0825)
results.authors: Gilbert MR, Dignam JJ, Armstrong TS, et al.
results.key_finding: Adding bevacizumab to standard temozolomide-radiotherapy did not improve overall survival in newly diagnosed GBM but increased progression-free survival and was associated with increased symptom burden.

results.title: Tumor treating fields (TTFields) plus temozolomide for newly diagnosed glioblastoma (EF-14 trial)
results.authors: Stupp R, Taillibert S, Kanner A, et al.
results.key_finding: TTFields added to maintenance temozolomide improved median OS to 20.9 months vs 16.0 months. Benefit was seen across subgroups including MGMT methylated tumors.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 (left temporal lobe)

differential.key_features: Same imaging differential pre-tissue; distinction made on histology (necrosis + microvascular proliferation define grade 4)
No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against
No fever or leukocytosis; DWI restriction at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus) and elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess
Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with imaging mass effect (effacement of ventricles / sulci / cisterns): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Imaging plans the approach and identifies the enhancing target to sample; biopsying before it risks a non-diagnostic specimen from a necrotic centre

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to control symptomatic peritumoral edema; titrate to lowest effective dose
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of intracranial mass effect — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a left temporal lobe heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Mass effect, even when modest, makes lumbar puncture risky and low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis — MRI must precede any consideration of LP
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate - 52-year-old woman with 2-month personality change and word-finding difficulty. MRI shows an irregular left temporal enhancing lesion without classic ring enhancement or necrosis, broadening the differential. Proximity to language cortex adds surgical complexity.
clinical_pearls: Not all glioblastomas present with the classic ring-enhancing pattern — irregular heterogeneous enhancement can also represent high-grade glioma, especially when perfusion and spectroscopy show aggressive features
Progressive word-finding difficulty in a previously articulate individual is a red flag for dominant temporal lobe pathology and should prompt urgent imaging
MGMT promoter methylation status is the strongest predictor of benefit from temozolomide chemotherapy in glioblastoma and should always be obtained
Functional MRI and intraoperative mapping are essential when tumors are near eloquent cortex to balance maximal resection (which improves survival) against functional preservation
